1 System Architecture

LanLink is a chat and file-transfer application for a local network, made of a server and a command-line client. One server runs on one host of the LAN. Each client keeps one TCP connection to it for the whole session, protected by TLS on the LAN. The server relays all traffic; clients never connect to each other.

1.1 Components and data paths

Figure 1 shows the server's accept loop, connection workers and shared registries, together with three clients and the UDP discovery path.

The server's main thread accepts TCP connections and starts one worker for each accepted socket. That worker performs the TLS handshake and the HELLO exchange, then handles authentication and later requests in its message loop. Running the handshake in the worker leaves the accept loop free to handle further connections, subject to the connection limit.

Workers share registries of connections, authenticated users and file transfers. When forwarding a message, the sending connection's worker looks up the recipient and writes to that recipient's socket through the connection transport.

A separate discovery thread answers UDP DISCOVER requests with SERVER_INFO. Discovery is optional: if the UDP port is unavailable because of a permission error or an address conflict, the server prints a warning and continues serving TCP clients.

The client has three persistent threads: the main thread handles commands and file events, the input thread reads typed commands, and the reader thread receives socket messages. Each accepted outgoing transfer starts a temporary sender thread. Table 2 in Section 1.3.1 gives their roles and responsibilities.

1.2 Layer separation

Layered organisation separates networking responsibilities [1]. Table 1 groups the modules into user-interface, network and data-processing layers.

Table 1. Layer separation: modules per layer.

Layer Modules
User interface client/__main__.py, client/display.py
Network common/transport.py, common/tls.py, common/handshake.py, client/connection.py, client/discovery.py, client/private_chat.py, server/app.py, server/discovery.py, server/sessions.py
Data processing common/protocol.py, common/builders.py, common/models.py, common/errors.py, transfer/*.py, server/auth.py

The codec and transfer engine contain no socket or TLS imports; the automated layering test checks this boundary. The transfer engine uses locks and cancellation flags but starts no threads. The network layer handles the HELLO exchange and dispatches incoming messages to the codec and transfer engines.

1.3 Concurrency model

The server uses blocking socket operations with timeouts and one worker per connection. The Python socket HOWTO describes using a separate thread to handle each accepted connection [2]. It allows up to 64 simultaneous connections by default and closes further sockets after accepting them. Workers release the shared registry lock before socket reads, writes or password hashing. A slow recipient can still delay workers forwarding to its connection.

1.3.1 Threads

Table 2 lists the threads used by the server and client. With N connection workers and discovery enabled, the server runs N + 2 threads. A logged-in CLI runs three persistent threads, plus one sender thread for each outgoing transfer that is sending.

Table 2. Threads on the server and the client.

Thread What it does How many
Server main thread Accept loop (0.1 s accept timeout); starts discovery and one worker per accepted socket; closes sockets above --max-clients; on shutdown, joins all workers 1
Server discovery thread Answers each valid DISCOVER with a unicast SERVER_INFO; daemon 0 or 1 (0 if the UDP bind fails)
Server connection worker TLS handshake, HELLO, login, request loop, cleanup; also writes forwarded chat and file messages onto other clients' connections; after HELLO, sets read-polling deadlines at most 0.5 s ahead 1 per connection, at most --max-clients (default 64)
Client main thread (login run) Command loop: takes one item at a time from the command/event queue (typed line, file event, final transfer snapshot); sends requests and waits for their replies 1
Client input thread Reads one stdin line per prompt and queues it; end of input becomes /logout; daemon 1
Client reader thread Only reader of the socket: prints chats, hands replies to waiting requests by ref_request_id, feeds file messages to the engines and sends their replies (e.g. FILE_RESULT), queues file events; not a daemon, joined when the client closes 1
Client file-sender thread Sends every FILE_CHUNK and the FILE_END; daemon 1 per accepted outgoing transfer
Client main thread (--discover or handshake-only run) One broadcast, collects SERVER_INFO replies for 2 s, exits; or one HELLO exchange, then exit 1

After HELLO, the worker's receive loop sets read deadlines no more than 0.5 s ahead. On a read timeout it checks transfer deadlines and whether the connection is closing. This polling supports connection cleanup during Windows operation (Section 4.3); time spent writing, processing messages or waiting for locks is outside the read deadline.

The concurrency test connects 20 clients and performs their HELLO exchanges in parallel, then checks that all 20 workers are alive. It uses plaintext loopback connections and does not measure an authenticated chat or file-transfer workload.

1.3.2 Locks and lock order

Table 3 identifies the locks, the data they protect and whether they are held during socket reads or writes.

Table 3. Locks, what they protect and whether they are held during socket I/O.

Lock Protects Held during socket I/O
Server registry lock connections, users and file transfers; connection state; transfer status and deadline; the atomic check-and-insert at login never while a thread reads or writes a socket or hashes a password (the accept loop does close an over-cap socket and start a worker under it)
Per-transfer lock the order in which one transfer's messages are checked and forwarded yes, while forwarding to the other party or sending ERROR to both
Connection write lock one sendall() of one whole frame yes (its purpose)
Client session lock pending requests, incoming offers, live transfers, the stored connection error never
Transfer-engine reentrant lock one transfer's client-side state never; callbacks run after it is released

When server locks are nested, the transfer lock comes before the registry or socket write lock. The registry lock is released before acquiring a transfer or write lock, and the write lock is held only around sendall(). On the client, the shared session lock and engine locks are not nested; engine callbacks run after the engine lock is released.

Several threads can write to the same connection. Each connection transport holds its write lock for one complete frame, preventing concurrent frames from interleaving. The concurrent-write test sends 400 frames from four threads through one connection and checks that they arrive intact.

A failed write may leave a partial frame on the recipient's stream. The server marks that connection CLOSING and shuts down its socket. The worker checks that state in its receive loop; the 0.5 s read-polling interval is not a guaranteed termination time.

1.4 Transport and security

TCP provides reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery [3], which suits LanLink's session, chat and file-transfer messages. UDP provides datagram delivery without reliability guarantees [4]. LanLink uses UDP for discovery, allowing a client to broadcast before it knows the server's address.

LAN connections use TLS 1.2 or newer through Python's standard ssl module [5]. The server loads its certificate and private key using --cert and --key. Clients load the server's self-signed certificate using --cafile and verify the server during the TLS handshake. Hostname checking is disabled because the server's LAN address may change. Without TLS, both programs restrict connections to loopback addresses.

TLS protects the full TCP stream, including login passwords, message headers and file data. UDP discovery is unencrypted and unauthenticated. A discovery reply does not establish trust: the subsequent TLS connection must pass certificate verification.

Password derivation uses PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 [6]. The account file stores the derived hashes with a random 16-byte salt and 600 000 iterations. The server uses hmac.compare_digest() to compare the derived and stored hashes. It also runs PBKDF2 for unknown usernames, using a dummy record. Three failed login attempts close the connection.

1.5 Scope and limitations

LanLink supports authenticated chat and server-relayed file transfer, but its presence and connection-monitoring features have the following limits.

  • Presence and user list. UDP discovery finds servers. Clients do not broadcast their presence, and the user list is requested after login and through /users. Changes in online users are not pushed to other clients.
  • Heartbeat. PING and PONG are defined in the codec but have no server handler. After login, sending PING produces an ERROR with code INVALID_FIELD, followed by disconnection. Connection cleanup relies on idle timeouts and I/O failures. The advertised heartbeat and idle values in HELLO_ACK are not applied by the client; Section 2.6.1 details the advertised and configured timeout values.

2 Protocol Specification

LanLink uses one application protocol, version 1. Chat, file and session messages travel as frames on one TCP connection per client, inside TLS when it is enabled (section 1.4). UDP carries only server discovery (2.8). The same schema check runs when a message is built, encoded and decoded, so neither side can send a message that breaks the field schema.

2.1 Design rationale

TCP delivers a byte stream, so one recv() can return part of a frame or several frames [2]. Instead of an end-of-message flag, every frame starts with the length of its header, and the header states the length of its payload. The receiver therefore always knows how many bytes it still needs, and file data needs no escaping. The header uses UTF-8 JSON [7]. LanLink encodes it with sorted keys and no spaces: it is readable in Wireshark on a plaintext loopback server, and the same message always gives the same bytes, so the tests compare frames byte for byte. The payload stays outside the JSON as raw bytes, so file chunks need no base64 (which adds one third) and the login password never appears in the header.

2.2 Frame format

2.2.1 Byte layout and byte order

Figure 2 shows one frame. The first 4 bytes are an unsigned 32-bit integer in big-endian (network) byte order. It gives N, the length of the JSON header in bytes, and counts neither itself nor the payload. N must be between 1 and 16 384. The header is N bytes of UTF-8 JSON, and its payload_length field gives P, the number of payload bytes that follow. P may be 0. The next frame starts immediately after the payload. The largest valid frame is a FILE_CHUNK or a USER_LIST reply, both with a 65 536-byte payload ceiling: 4 + 16 384 + 65 536 = 81 924 bytes.

2.2.2 How a receiver reads a frame

The receiver reads up to 64 KiB per recv() and feeds whatever arrives to a frame decoder. The decoder collects bytes in three stages and keeps any leftover bytes for the next stage:

  1. Exactly 4 bytes of prefix. They are decoded as N and checked: 0 gives BAD_FRAME, and more than 16 384 gives HEADER_TOO_LARGE. The check happens before any header byte is buffered.
  2. Exactly N bytes of header. They are parsed as strict JSON and validated against the schema of their type and direction (2.3, 2.4). The payload ceiling is checked here too, so a peer cannot make the receiver buffer more payload than the limit allows.
  3. Exactly payload_length bytes of payload. They are checked against the type (for example strict UTF-8 for chat), and the complete message is returned.

Several frames can complete in one recv(), and one frame can span many. After any protocol error the decoder is "poisoned": every later call raises the same error, because the position of the next frame boundary is no longer known. The stream is never resynchronised. End of stream exactly at a frame boundary is a clean close. End of stream inside a frame gives UNEXPECTED_EOF.

2.2.3 Worked example: a CHAT_PRIVATE frame

Listing 1 shows the real bytes the encoder produces when a client sends the text Hi Binh! privately to user binh. The request_id is fixed at r1 so that the output can be reproduced; a real client uses a random UUID in hex. The prefix 00 00 00 5b gives N = 91 header bytes (offsets 0x04 to 0x5e). The header has payload_length 8, so the payload is the 8 bytes at offsets 0x5f to 0x66, and the frame is 103 bytes long. The keys appear in sorted order because encoding is canonical.

2.3 Common header fields and identifier formats

Every header carries the four common fields in Table 4. A reply also carries ref_request_id.

Table 4. Common header fields.

Field JSON type Required Meaning and format
version integer every message Protocol version. It must be 1, otherwise UNSUPPORTED_VERSION.
type string every message One of the 21 message types. An unknown value gives UNKNOWN_TYPE.
request_id string every message ID of this message: 1 to 64 characters from A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -. The client and server use a random UUID in hex.
payload_length integer every message Number of payload bytes after the header, from 0 to the ceiling of the type (Table 11, Section 2.6.1).
ref_request_id string replies (per type, Tables 5 to 9) The request_id of the message being answered. Same format as request_id.

A transfer_id is 32 lowercase hex characters and a sha256 is 64. Validation is strict. The field set must be exact: a missing field gives MISSING_FIELD and an extra one INVALID_FIELD. Integers must be JSON integers (not booleans), strings must be non-empty without control characters, and duplicate keys, NaN or Infinity give BAD_JSON. String lengths are in Table 11 (Section 2.6.1), and the codec enforces the field rules described above.

The receiver also checks direction. HELLO and AUTH come only from a client; HELLO_ACK, AUTH_OK, ERROR and CHAT_ACK only from the server; DISCOVER and SERVER_INFO only over UDP. A type in the wrong direction gives INVALID_FIELD.

2.4 Message catalogue

There are 21 message types, 19 on TCP and 2 on UDP, listed by group in Tables 5 to 9. "opt." marks an optional field; every other listed field is required. A type without a listed payload must have an empty payload. Section 3 shows the order of messages in a conversation.

2.4.1 Session

Table 5. Session messages.

Type Direction Header fields (besides common) Payload Reply
HELLO C→S client_name (≤64), client_version (≤32) none HELLO_ACK
HELLO_ACK S→C ref_request_id, server_name (≤64), limits (object with exactly the 8 limit keys listed in Section 2.6.1) none none
AUTH C→S username (≤32, no whitespace) password, UTF-8, 1–256 B AUTH_OK, or ERROR
AUTH_OK S→C ref_request_id, username none none
USER_LIST request C→S none must be empty USER_LIST reply, or ERROR
USER_LIST reply S→C ref_request_id JSON {"users":[{"username","online","ip","port"}]}, 1–65 536 B none
LOGOUT C→S opt. reason (≤128) none After login: none; the server closes the connection. Before login: ERROR NOT_AUTHENTICATED, and the connection stays open
PING either (unused) none none PONG (never sent)
PONG either (unused) ref_request_id none none

The client checks that the limits object in HELLO_ACK is valid (an invalid one fails the handshake) but never applies the values (see 1.5). In the USER_LIST reply, ip and port may be null. PING and PONG have no handler: a client that sends PING gets an ERROR and is disconnected (Table 10; see 1.5).

2.4.2 Chat

Table 6. Chat messages.

Type Direction Header fields (besides common) Payload Reply
CHAT_PUBLIC C→S none UTF-8 text, 1–8 192 B CHAT_ACK
CHAT_PUBLIC forwarded S→C sender, message_id, timestamp_ms same text none
CHAT_PRIVATE C→S recipient (≤32) UTF-8 text, 1–8 192 B CHAT_ACK, or ERROR
CHAT_PRIVATE forwarded S→C recipient, sender, message_id, timestamp_ms same text none
CHAT_ACK S→C ref_request_id, message_id, timestamp_ms, status (must be "accepted") none none

The forwarded copy has a new request_id and the server-stamped sender, message_id and timestamp_ms (Unix milliseconds; 2.6.3). The same message_id and timestamp_ms return in CHAT_ACK, which means "accepted by the server", not "delivered": a public message is acknowledged even if there were no recipients or some deliveries failed.

2.4.3 File transfer

Table 7. File-transfer messages. "Sender" and "recipient" are the two clients of a transfer. Every message passes through the server.

Type Sent by Header fields (besides common) Payload Server action
FILE_OFFER sender transfer_id, recipient, filename, size, sha256, chunk_size; the forwarded copy adds sender none Creates an OFFERED session and forwards the offer to the recipient, or replies ERROR
FILE_ACCEPT recipient transfer_id none Sets ACCEPTED, forwards to the sender, then echoes back to the recipient
FILE_REJECT recipient transfer_id; opt. reason (≤128, free text) none Sets REJECTED, forwards to the sender, then echoes back to the recipient
FILE_CHUNK sender transfer_id, seq file bytes, 1–65 536 B Relays it, sets TRANSFERRING
FILE_END sender transfer_id, total_chunks, total_bytes none Relays it, sets VERIFYING
FILE_RESULT recipient transfer_id, ok, received_bytes; opt. sha256, opt. error_code none Relays it, sets COMPLETED or FAILED
FILE_CANCEL either transfer_id; opt. reason (must be an error code) none Relays it, sets CANCELLED

The decoder rejects a filename that is not 1–255 characters and at most 255 UTF-8 bytes, is . or .., or contains / or \, with UNSAFE_FILENAME, and any size above 100 MiB with FILE_TOO_LARGE. chunk_size must be 1–65 536, and FILE_RESULT carries error_code exactly when ok is false.

The server does not check seq, sizes or hashes; the receiving client does. seq must be the next chunk number (SEQ_MISMATCH). Every chunk but the last must be chunk_size bytes, and the totals in FILE_END must match (SIZE_MISMATCH). The SHA-256 of the received bytes must match the offer (HASH_MISMATCH). The receiver always puts that hash in FILE_RESULT, and the sender accepts ok: true only if received_bytes and the hash match its own file.

2.4.4 Discovery

Table 8. Discovery messages (UDP only; the datagram format is in 2.8).

Type Direction Header fields (besides common) Payload Reply
DISCOVER client → broadcast none none SERVER_INFO
SERVER_INFO server → client (unicast) ref_request_id, server_name (≤64), port (1–65535), tls (bool); opt. host (≤255) none none

The server never sets host; the client takes the server's IP from the datagram's source address. Either type sent over TCP gives INVALID_FIELD.

2.4.5 Error

Table 9. The error message.

Type Direction Header fields (besides common) Payload Reply
ERROR S→C only code (an error code, Table 10), message (≤256); opt. ref_request_id, opt. field (≤64), opt. transfer_id none none

message is user-facing text (Vietnamese, except one English text in the HELLO phase). ref_request_id is present when the error answers a request. It is absent from the HELLO-phase error and from transfer notices (TIMEOUT, CONNECTION_LOST), including the one the recipient gets when its FILE_REJECT cannot be forwarded. The server never sets field.

2.5 Error codes

There are 35 error codes. A code reaches the peer in an ERROR, as the error_code of a FILE_RESULT, or as the reason of a FILE_CANCEL. Decoder errors close the connection without a reply (2.6.2), and some codes are local only.

Table 10 lists all 35 error codes, where each can appear (ERROR.code, FILE_RESULT.error_code, FILE_CANCEL.reason, a closed connection, or a local outcome only) and when it is produced.

Table 10. Error codes and where each appears on the wire.

Code Where it appears When
BAD_FRAME connection closed; datagram ignored (UDP) Header length 0; a UDP datagram with bytes after its frame
HEADER_TOO_LARGE connection closed Header length above 16 384 B
PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE connection closed; datagram ignored (UDP) payload_length above the ceiling for the type; datagram above 1 024 B
PAYLOAD_LENGTH_MISMATCH local only A locally constructed message whose payload size differs from payload_length (only at build or encode time, because the decoder always reads exactly payload_length bytes)
UNEXPECTED_EOF connection closed; datagram ignored (UDP) Stream ends inside a frame; datagram shorter than its prefix says
BAD_JSON connection closed; local Invalid UTF-8 or JSON, header not an object, duplicate key, NaN/Infinity, or nesting too deep for the JSON parser. Local: a header nested deeper than 32 at build or encode time (a received header nested that deep fails the field checks first, with INVALID_FIELD)
UNSUPPORTED_VERSION connection closed version is not 1
UNKNOWN_TYPE connection closed type is not one of the supported message types
MISSING_FIELD connection closed A required field is absent
INVALID_FIELD connection closed; ERROR Decoder: bad value, unknown field or wrong direction (closed). ERROR: first message is not HELLO; HELLO, PING or PONG after login (then closed; before login these get NOT_AUTHENTICATED, then closed); FILE_OFFER to oneself
SPOOFED_FIELD connection closed A client header contains sender, message_id or timestamp_ms
BAD_PAYLOAD connection closed Empty AUTH, chat or FILE_CHUNK payload; text that is not UTF-8; malformed USER_LIST JSON
NOT_AUTHENTICATED ERROR Any message other than AUTH before login
AUTH_FAILED ERROR Wrong username or password, or the server was started without --users. The third failure also closes the connection
ALREADY_LOGGED_IN ERROR AUTH on a connection that is already logged in, or for a username that has a session
RECIPIENT_OFFLINE ERROR CHAT_PRIVATE or FILE_OFFER to a username with no active session, whether or not the account exists
RECIPIENT_UNKNOWN never raised Defined, but no code path uses it
QUEUE_FULL ERROR; local ERROR: the connection has already used 64 transfer IDs. Local: the client already has 64 requests waiting for replies; or the client's file-event queue is full, which closes the client's connection. That queue defaults to 128 entries, but the CLI passes its own unbounded queue, so this case cannot occur in the CLI
TIMEOUT ERROR A transfer phase exceeded --transfer-timeout; sent with transfer_id to both parties
CONNECTION_LOST ERROR; local ERROR reply to CHAT_PRIVATE when the write to the recipient failed, and to CHAT_PRIVATE/FILE_OFFER when the recipient's AUTH_OK was not sent within 1 s. ERROR notice with transfer_id and no ref_request_id, sent to both parties, when the other party of a transfer disconnected or a transfer message (including the FILE_OFFER itself) could not be forwarded. The exception is a FILE_RESULT or FILE_CANCEL that ends the transfer: if it cannot be forwarded, it is dropped without a notice. If a FILE_REJECT could not be forwarded, the notice goes to the recipient only. Local: the client lost the server
FILE_TOO_LARGE connection closed; local Decoder: a size field above 100 MiB. Local: source-file inspection refuses to offer the file
FILE_NOT_FOUND local Source-file inspection finds that the path is missing or is not a regular file
SOURCE_CHANGED FILE_CANCEL.reason; local Local: the file changed while it was being hashed before the offer. FILE_CANCEL.reason: it changed while the chunks were being sent
UNSAFE_FILENAME connection closed; local Decoder: bad filename. Local: filename validation
TRANSFER_UNKNOWN ERROR transfer_id not registered, already finished, or expired on accept or reject
TRANSFER_STATE ERROR; FILE_RESULT.error_code ERROR: duplicate transfer_id, wrong party, or a message not allowed in the current status. Result: the receiver got an unexpected message
SEQ_MISMATCH FILE_RESULT.error_code Chunk seq is not the next expected number
SIZE_MISMATCH FILE_RESULT.error_code; local A chunk or total size is wrong. The sender also fails locally if received_bytes differs from the file size
HASH_MISMATCH FILE_RESULT.error_code; local The SHA-256 of the received bytes differs from the offer, or the result hash differs from the sender's
DISK_FULL FILE_RESULT.error_code No space while writing. At accept time, the client sends FILE_REJECT (no reason) instead
PERMISSION_DENIED FILE_RESULT.error_code No permission while writing or renaming. At accept time, the client sends FILE_REJECT instead
REJECTED_BY_PEER local The sender's outcome after FILE_REJECT
CANCELLED_BY_PEER local The outcome after receiving FILE_CANCEL
CANCELLED_LOCAL local; FILE_CANCEL.reason Local cancellation through the transfer-engine API. The CLI has no cancel command
INTERNAL FILE_RESULT.error_code; local Any other OS error; fallback text for an unknown code

RECIPIENT_UNKNOWN is never raised: the server looks only for an active session, so a message to an unknown username gets RECIPIENT_OFFLINE. FILE_CANCEL.reason carries whichever error stopped the sender while it was reading the file; in practice SOURCE_CHANGED or a translated OS error.

2.6 Limits and validation

2.6.1 Key limits

The largest frame is 81 924 B (4 + 16 384 + 65 536). A file chunk carries at most 64 KiB (65 536 B), a chat message at most 8 KiB (8 192 B), and a file may be at most 100 MiB. An idle connection is closed after 45 s with the server's built-in default, or 120 s when the server is started from the command line. A new connection has 5 s for the TLS handshake and then a fresh 5 s to send HELLO.

Table 11 collects every size limit and timeout. The size values are the protocol defaults. A decoded limits object must contain exactly the eight keys below. Each value must stay within a ceiling (for example 1 MiB for the header and chunk limits, 65 507 B for datagrams), and the idle timeout must be greater than the heartbeat interval.

max_header_bytes      max_chunk_bytes       max_file_bytes     max_chat_bytes
max_user_list_bytes   max_datagram_bytes    heartbeat_interval_s   idle_timeout_s

Table 11. Size limits and timeouts.

Item Value Effect
Header length N 1–16 384 B BAD_FRAME / HEADER_TOO_LARGE
AUTH payload 1–256 B PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE / BAD_PAYLOAD
Chat payload 1–8 192 B same
FILE_CHUNK payload, chunk_size 1–65 536 B same; INVALID_FIELD for chunk_size
USER_LIST payload request 0 B; reply 1–65 536 B same
Payload of every other type 0 B PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE
File size 0–104 857 600 B (100 MiB) FILE_TOO_LARGE
UDP datagram (whole frame) ≤ 1 024 B PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE; datagram ignored
String fields (characters) username, sender, recipient 32 (no whitespace); client_name 64; client_version 32; server_name 64; host 255; message 256; field 64; status 16; reason 128; filename 255 (and ≤255 UTF-8 bytes); ip 45 INVALID_FIELD / UNSAFE_FILENAME / BAD_PAYLOAD
Integers 0 to 2^63-1; port 1–65535 INVALID_FIELD
Transfer IDs per connection 64 QUEUE_FULL
Failed logins per connection 3 connection closed
Concurrent connections (--max-clients) 64 extra connections closed at once
Handshake (server --timeout) 5.0 s for the TLS handshake, then a fresh 5.0 s for HELLO connection closed, no ERROR
Idle connection (--idle-timeout) 45.0 s (server class default); 120.0 s (--idle-timeout) connection closed; extended while the connection has a live transfer
Transfer phase (--transfer-timeout) 60.0 s ERROR TIMEOUT to both parties; reset by every accepted or relayed transfer message
Worker wake-up 0.5 s longest single wait in recv(); worker re-checks transfer deadlines and CLOSING
Wait for recipient's AUTH_OK 1.0 s ERROR CONNECTION_LOST
Heartbeat interval 15 s advertised only; nothing uses it
Client request (client --timeout) 5.0 s waits for the matching reply; on expiry the client closes the session
Discovery wait 2.0 s collects SERVER_INFO replies until then
Transfer engine timeouts sender 60 s (OFFERED) / 30 s (later); receiver 30 s available in the transfer engine but not activated by the CLI

The advertised idle timeout differs from the real one: HELLO_ACK always advertises 45 s (the built-in server default), while the command-line server uses 120 s. The client checks that limits is valid (an invalid object fails the handshake) but never applies the values, so the wrong number has no effect at run time.

2.6.2 Malformed frame vs. bad request

Malformed frame: the connection is closed. Any decoder error (framing, JSON, schema, direction or a spoofed field) poisons the stream (2.2.2), so the server closes the socket without a reply. The only exception is a well-formed frame other than HELLO during the HELLO phase: it gets ERROR INVALID_FIELD without ref_request_id, and then the connection closes. A handshake timeout closes silently.

Valid frame, bad request: an ERROR reply. A well-formed message that fails a routing, state or login check gets one ERROR with the code, ref_request_id and, if present, transfer_id. The connection stays open, except after the third AUTH_FAILED and after an unhandled type (HELLO after the handshake, PING, PONG). Table 10 gives the codes. Invalid UDP datagrams are ignored silently.

2.6.3 Server-stamped fields

sender, message_id and timestamp_ms are set only by the server. If a client header contains any of them, the frame fails with SPOOFED_FIELD and the connection closes. The server stamps sender (the username logged in on the sending connection) on every forwarded chat message and FILE_OFFER, and a fresh message_id and timestamp_ms on chat messages. A client therefore cannot claim to be another user.

2.7 State diagrams

2.7.1 Server-side connection

The server keeps one record per accepted socket; Figure 3 shows its states.

  • CONNECTING: created after accept() if fewer than the maximum number of clients (64 by default) are connected; TLS handshake, then HELLO, 5 s each.
  • HELLO_ACCEPTED: HELLO_ACK sent; the server waits for AUTH.
  • AUTHENTICATED: user registered, then AUTH_OK sent; other users' messages are forwarded only after that AUTH_OK (waiting up to 1 s).
  • CLOSING: server shutdown, or a failed write to this peer (a partial frame may be on the wire); nothing more is sent, and the worker notices within 0.5 s.
  • CLOSED: every exit path; the user is removed and its transfers fail with CONNECTION_LOST.

End of stream, an idle timeout, a malformed frame, the third failed login, an unhandled type and LOGOUT after login go straight to CLOSED. Before login, LOGOUT gets ERROR NOT_AUTHENTICATED and the state does not change.

2.7.2 File transfer

A transfer has eight statuses, four of them final (COMPLETED, REJECTED, FAILED, CANCELLED). The sender, the server and the recipient each track it. Figure 4 shows the allowed transitions; every non-final state may also move to CANCELLED or FAILED.

  • OFFERED: the offer is made (sender, server); the recipient's record starts here when its user accepts.
  • ACCEPTED: the recipient has opened its .part file and sends FILE_ACCEPT.
  • TRANSFERRING: chunks are flowing (from the first FILE_CHUNK).
  • VERIFYING: the last chunk is sent and FILE_END follows.
  • COMPLETED: counts and SHA-256 match and the .part file is renamed; FILE_RESULT with ok: true.
  • REJECTED / CANCELLED: after FILE_REJECT / FILE_CANCEL.
  • FAILED: ERROR TIMEOUT or CONNECTION_LOST, FILE_RESULT with ok: false, or a local error.

The server also checks roles. Only the recipient may send FILE_ACCEPT or FILE_REJECT (in OFFERED) and FILE_RESULT (after OFFERED; ok: true only in VERIFYING). Only the sender may send FILE_CHUNK or FILE_END (in ACCEPTED or TRANSFERRING). Either party may send FILE_CANCEL before a final state. Anything else gets ERROR TRANSFER_STATE, and a finished session is removed at once.

Unlike the two clients, the server does not check transitions on its relay path. Its record therefore also moves TRANSFERRING → TRANSFERRING on each further chunk, and ACCEPTED → VERIFYING for an empty file (marked in Figure 4).

2.8 UDP discovery

A client finds a server on the LAN by UDP broadcast. Each datagram holds exactly one frame in the format of Figure 2, with no payload and no trailing bytes, and is at most 1 024 B long; an invalid datagram is ignored.

The server binds its UDP socket to the same address and port as its TCP listener (default port 5000; with the default host 127.0.0.1 this is loopback). If the bind fails, the server runs without discovery. The client broadcasts one DISCOVER to 255.255.255.255 on that port and collects replies for 2 s. The server answers with a unicast SERVER_INFO to the source address and port of the request, carrying ref_request_id, server_name, the TCP port and the tls flag.

The client keeps the replies that match its request_id, takes each server's IP from the source address, prints the list and exits. The user then connects with that host and port; TLS is chosen from the client's own options, not from tls. Discovery is plaintext and finds servers, not users (see 1.5); a client learns who is online through USER_LIST (Table 5).

3 Sequence Diagrams

This section follows a chat message and a file transfer through the system. In Figures 5 to 9 one lifeline is one thread, not one host: the server has a main thread that accepts connections and one worker thread per client, and each client has a main thread, a keyboard thread, a reader thread and, while it sends a file, a file-sender thread (Table 2, Section 1.3.1). The server has no central router thread. The worker of the connection that sent a message writes the forwarded copy straight into the recipient's socket; a write lock per socket keeps this frame from interleaving with the recipient worker's own replies. Error codes are listed in Table 10 (Section 2.5), limits and timeouts in Table 11 (Section 2.6.1), and the connection and transfer states in Figures 3 and 4.

3.1 Login and user list

Figure 5 shows how a client connects, logs in and fetches the first user list.

  1. The server's main thread accepts the TCP connection and starts a worker for it, or closes it at once if 64 connections are already open.
  2. With TLS on, the handshake runs in the worker, so a slow client never blocks the accept loop.
  3. The client sends HELLO, the worker answers HELLO_ACK, and the connection becomes HELLO_ACCEPTED.
  4. The client sends AUTH with the username in the header and the password in the payload.
  5. The worker checks the PBKDF2 hash, registers the session, enters AUTHENTICATED and replies AUTH_OK; only then may other workers forward messages to this client.
  6. The client starts its reader thread and asks for USER_LIST, which lists every online user with IP address and port.

The TLS handshake and HELLO each get 5 s; on expiry the server closes the socket without an ERROR. A bad password gets an ERROR with AUTH_FAILED, and a name already online gets ALREADY_LOGGED_IN. The CLI then exits; the server itself closes a connection after three failed logins.

3.2 Chat message lifecycle

Figure 6 follows one private message from Alice to Bob.

  1. Alice types /msg bob hi; her client sends CHAT_PRIVATE with a fresh request_id and recipient = bob, and waits for the reply.
  2. Alice's server worker finds Bob among the logged-in users and waits up to 1 s until his own AUTH_OK has been sent.
  3. The worker stamps the fields a client may not set: sender, a new message_id and the server's timestamp_ms. A client frame that contains them fails with SPOOFED_FIELD and the connection is closed (2.6.3).
  4. The worker writes the stamped message directly into Bob's socket, and Bob's reader thread prints it; Bob's server worker is not involved.
  5. Only after that write succeeds does the worker send CHAT_ACK to Alice, carrying her request ID in ref_request_id and the server's message ID and timestamp.

CHAT_ACK means "written to Bob's connection", not "read by Bob". If Bob has no session, Alice gets ERROR RECIPIENT_OFFLINE. If the write to Bob fails, his stream may hold a partial frame, so the server shuts his socket down (his worker exits within 0.5 s) and answers Alice with ERROR CONNECTION_LOST, as it also does when Bob's AUTH_OK is not out within 1 s.

A public message (/all hi, type CHAT_PUBLIC, no recipient field) is handled differently, as the note at the bottom of Figure 6 shows. Alice's worker delivers it to each other online user one by one, closing and skipping any recipient whose write fails. It then always sends CHAT_ACK, even with no recipients, so this ack only means "accepted" (best effort).

3.3 File transfer: happy path

Figure 7 shows a successful transfer: negotiation, chunk stream, verification.

  1. Alice types /offer bob a.pdf; her client reads the file once for its size and SHA-256 and sends FILE_OFFER with these values, the file name and the chunk size.
  2. Alice's worker creates a transfer session in state OFFERED and forwards the offer to Bob with sender added.
  3. Bob types /accept <id>; his client creates a private temporary .part file and only then sends FILE_ACCEPT.
  4. Bob's worker moves the session to ACCEPTED and forwards the accept to Alice, whose reader thread starts a file-sender thread so that the reader stays free.
  5. The sender thread sends FILE_CHUNK messages of up to 64 KiB with seq = 0 … n−1 and the raw bytes as payload, then FILE_END with the chunk and byte totals.
  6. Alice's worker relays each message to Bob without reading the data, moving the session to TRANSFERRING and then VERIFYING.
  7. Bob's reader checks each chunk's seq and size, appends it to the .part file and updates a running SHA-256 digest [8].
  8. On FILE_END, Bob's client checks the counts and the digest against the offer, flushes the file to disk and renames it to its final name in one atomic step.
  9. Bob sends FILE_RESULT with ok = true; his worker marks the session COMPLETED and forwards it, and Alice's client checks size and hash once more.

There is no per-chunk acknowledgement. TCP already delivers the bytes in order, and its flow control paces the sender: if Bob reads slowly, the write to his socket blocks Alice's worker, which stops reading from Alice, whose sender thread then blocks on its own write. Thanks to the .part file and the final rename, an incomplete or corrupt download never appears under the real name.

3.4 File transfer: failure paths

Figure 8 shows the two deliberate stops.

  • Reject. Bob's FILE_REJECT is forwarded to Alice, the session ends REJECTED, and no file is opened and no sender thread started.
  • Cancel. The CLI has no cancel command: FILE_CANCEL is sent only when reading the source fails mid-transfer (e.g. SOURCE_CHANGED), and Bob's client then deletes its .part file and ends CANCELLED.

Figure 9 shows the failures nobody chose. In each case the transfer ends FAILED and the receiver deletes its .part file.

  • Disconnect. When either party's connection drops, the server sends the other one an ERROR with CONNECTION_LOST and the transfer ID.
  • Hash mismatch. If Bob's digest differs from the offer, he sends FILE_RESULT with ok = false and HASH_MISMATCH; a wrong seq or chunk size fails the same way at once.
  • Timeout. If no message is relayed for 60 s, the first worker to notice (each wakes at least every 0.5 s) sends ERROR TIMEOUT to both clients.

3.5 Matching replies to requests

Every request carries a fresh request_id, and its direct reply, including an ERROR it causes, repeats that value in ref_request_id. After login the client keeps one waiting slot per request and the reader thread fills the slot that matches each reply, so concurrent requests never get each other's answers. An unmatched reply, or no reply within 5 s, closes the connection, and at most 64 requests can wait at once. Chat, file messages and errors that name a transfer are not replies and go straight to the screen or the transfer code.

4 Challenges & Solutions

LanLink required careful handling of TCP framing, concurrent access, failed connections and forwarding delays. These challenges led to the following design decisions and failure-handling improvements.

4.1 Preserving message boundaries and write integrity

TCP delivers a byte stream: one read may contain part of a frame or several frames. Concurrent writers also need coordination to avoid mixing frame bytes. LanLink uses the length-prefixed format in Section 2.2, retains incomplete data between reads and stops decoding after a corrupt frame. A per-connection write lock protects each complete send. Tests check decoding at every split point of a three-frame stream and verify that 400 frames written by four threads arrive intact.

4.2 Coordinating shared state without deadlock

Server workers share registries and per-transfer locks. Inconsistent lock ordering could cause deadlock; socket I/O under the registry lock could delay unrelated clients. When locks are nested, the transfer lock comes before the registry lock, as described in Section 1.3.2. Workers release the registry lock before socket reads or writes. A client cleanup test checks the related rule that its shared lock stays available during socket shutdown; it does not establish that all server deadlocks are impossible.

4.3 Cleaning up failed connections

An earlier client failure path could leave its reader thread running after disconnection. Windows testing also exposed delayed removal of a peer after a forwarding failure. The client now closes its socket on the first failure and wakes pending requests. The server marks a failed recipient CLOSING and shuts down its socket. Workers check state using read-polling intervals of at most 0.5 seconds, without guaranteeing cleanup within that time. The forwarding-failure test checks CONNECTION_LOST and peer removal within three seconds.

4.4 Reducing delays before chat acknowledgment

Public chat forwards to recipients sequentially before acknowledging the sender. Waiting for a recipient's authentication response could therefore contribute to a sender timeout. The authentication-readiness wait is now limited to one second per recipient instead of the longer idle timeout. This reduces one source of delay, but waits and blocking writes can still accumulate. The existing timeout test covers the private-message route, not public-broadcast timing. The change is therefore a partial improvement; slow-recipient isolation remains future work.

5 Testing

5.1 Automated tests

The tests run under pytest and otherwise use only the Python standard library, like the application. They cover the frame codec, the file engine, and integration tests that start a real server on the loopback interface and connect real client sockets to it. A run of the 550 tests (counting parametrised cases) on Windows gave 548 passed and 2 skipped; both skipped tests need file-system features that host lacks. Table 12 summarizes the test coverage.

Table 12. Test areas.

Test area What it checks
Framing A stream split at every byte offset decodes to the same frames.
Wire format Golden frames match byte for byte; invalid ones fail with their error code.
Concurrency: server 20 clients connect and send HELLO at once; each gets its own worker.
Concurrency: one socket 400 frames written from 4 threads through one connection all arrive whole.
Resilience: disconnect A client that resets its connection is removed; new clients are still accepted.
Resilience: forwarding A failed forward gives the sender CONNECTION_LOST; the peer goes offline.
Resilience: shutdown Server shutdown ends every client reader and leaves no users or connections.
File integrity Bad or out-of-order chunks give HASH_MISMATCH or SEQ_MISMATCH; no file is left.
Auth and TLS A client refuses a server certificate it does not trust.
Discovery Junk datagrams are ignored and DISCOVER is still answered.
CLI An incoming message is printed while the client waits for input.

5.2 User interface

The client is a command-line program with no GUI toolkit (Figure 10). Incoming chat appears at once on its own line as [sender -> recipient] text, where the recipient is all for a public message. The user list shows Online users (N): and then one line per user with the name and the IP address and port, with (you) on the user's own line. During a transfer, both sides redraw one line in place with a bar, the percentage, the file name, the peer and the bytes done, for example [#####...............] 25% a.txt to bob 256/1024 B. The commands are:

  • /msg USER TEXT: private message
  • /all TEXT: public message
  • /offer USER PATH: offer a file
  • /accept ID, /reject ID [REASON]: answer an offer
  • /users or Enter: show the online users
  • /logout or Ctrl+D: log out

5.3 Manual demo

The demo in Figure 11 uses one host and four terminals: create accounts for alice, bob and charlie, start the server in one terminal, and start one client per user in the others (replace NAME with the username).

python -m server.auth --file data/users.json --username alice
python -m server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5000 --users data/users.json
python -m client --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5000 --username NAME

6 Conclusion

LanLink provides authenticated private and public chat, an online user list and file transfer through a central server. Clients keep a TCP connection for their session, use TLS when communicating across the LAN, and can find the server through optional UDP discovery. File transfers include recipient approval and checks of the received size and SHA-256 digest before completion is confirmed.

Building the application showed how much coordination is needed above the transport layer. The application must define message boundaries, match replies to requests, protect shared state and handle interrupted connections without leaving unfinished transfers behind. Separating the interface, networking and transfer logic made these behaviours easier to test. The automated tests cover framing, concurrent connections, authentication, file integrity and failure handling, while the terminal demonstration shows private chat, public chat and a completed file transfer.

The current version is intended for live communication between online users. Public messages are forwarded to recipients in sequence, discovery has no retry, and there is no heartbeat or storage for offline messages. Future work could improve connection monitoring, make discovery less sensitive to packet loss and reduce the effect of a slow recipient on public chat. These improvements would extend the existing design without changing the basic client-server model.
